arguments.heading: Argument session of March 2, 2026
paragraphs: The government's side, argued by Ms. Harris, asked the Court to uphold the charge under the unlawful user prong. She argued the law is constitutional as applied to habitual illegal drug users, relying on historical analogues like habitual drunkards, vagrancy, civil commitment, and surety laws. She said the ban is temporary and within the user's control. She also asserted the law embodies Congress's judgment that gun possession by habitual users or addicts is dangerous, citing Heller for category-based restrictions.

Hemani's side, argued by Ms. Murphy, asked the Court to affirm the decision below. She said facial versus as-applied grounds are not critical. She agreed categorical prohibitions may be permissible but insisted the government must prove under Bruen that any drug-based ban maps onto historical tradition. She argued the unlawful user prong is unconstitutionally vague for lack of fair notice. She said deferring to congressional findings alone would abandon Bruen's historical analogue requirement.

Ms. Murphy also contended historical tradition supports disarming drug addicts and called that the dominant modern state approach. She invited a narrow ruling that the government cannot prevail by showing only that a person uses an unknown quantity of marijuana a few times a week. She agreed tradition supports restrictions on addicts, citing addiction as an analogue to habitual drunkards.

The justices tested several assumptions. Justice Gorsuch asked whether minimal, regular marijuana use qualifies as unlawful use subject to disarmament. Justice Barrett asked what evidence supports that regular marijuana use increases dangerousness. Justice Alito asked whether illegal drugs were part of the historical landscape and whether alcohol is different. Justice Thomas asked what public safety concerns justified disarming other vagrancy categories beyond drunkards.

Justice Jackson asked for the specific founding-era attribute of habitual drunkards that parallels an every-other-day marijuana user. She also challenged the government's attempt to equate founding-era habitual drunkards with modern habitual drug users by redefining terms. These questions probed whether the government's historical analogues truly match the modern drug user category.

Ms. Harris answered that illegal drug use per se lacks founding-era guidance and that alcohol differs historically. She conceded that minimal but habitual illegal drug use can trigger the law under the government's view. She also conceded that habitual unlawful use suffices regardless of proximity to a firearm. No reargument occurred in this session, so nothing was revisited on that basis.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case is called United States v. Ali Danial Hemani. It tests a federal law that bans gun possession by people who use illegal drugs. The key question is whether that ban can constitutionally apply to Hemani himself.
Federal law, called Section 922(g)(3), makes it a crime for an unlawful drug user to have a gun. Hemani says the law cannot be applied to him. The government defends the charge.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Court heard oral argument on March 2, 2026, in Washington, D.C., starting at 10:04 a.m. Sarah M. Harris argued for the government, which is the the side that brought the case here. Erin E. Murphy argued for Hemani, the the opposing side.
The Chief Justice noted that Ms. Harris began the argument for the government. At the end, the Chief Justice said the case was submitted after the argument concluded.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Hemani's lawyer asked the Court to uphold the decision below. She said whether the ruling is facial or as-applied is not critical to her side. A facial ruling strikes the whole law; an as-applied ruling strikes it only for this person.
The government's lawyer defended the charge under the unlawful user prong of the law. That prong targets people who use illegal drugs, rather than a separate prong about addiction.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues the law is constitutional as applied to habitual illegal drug users. It points to old laws about habitual drunkards, vagrancy, civil commitment, and surety laws as historical analogues. It also says the ban is temporary and within the user's control.

Hemani's side agrees categorical bans may be allowed, but insists the government must prove the ban maps onto historical tradition under Bruen. Bruen is a case requiring modern gun laws to match old traditions. She also argues the unlawful user prong is unconstitutionally vague, giving no fair notice.

Hemani's side says deferring to congressional findings alone would abandon Bruen's historical analogue requirement. She contends historical tradition supports disarming drug addicts, and that this is the dominant modern state approach. She also invited a narrow ruling that the government cannot win by showing only that a person uses an unknown amount of marijuana a few times a week.

The government's lawyer separately asserted that the law embodies Congress's judgment that gun possession by habitual users or addicts is dangerous. She cited Heller as recognizing category-based restrictions for special dangers of misuse.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The case tests how far Bruen's history-based test reaches. Bruen requires modern gun laws to match historical traditions. The justices' questions show the fight turns on comparing old categories, like habitual drunkards, with modern drug use.

Both sides also addressed how much proof matters. The government leaned on Congress's judgment about dangerousness. Hemani's side said Congress's findings alone cannot replace the required historical comparison.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: The case was submitted at the conclusion of argument. That means the justices will meet privately and vote later. The approved record does not support any prediction about the outcome.
A question from a justice is not a holding or a vote. Nothing in the argument session shows how the Court will rule.
